cards.front: What does a single artificial neuron compute?
cards.back: y = σ(Σ wᵢxᵢ + b) — weighted sum of inputs plus bias, then a non-linearity σ.

cards.front: Why is a non-linearity required between linear layers?
cards.back: Without it, stacking layers collapses to a single linear transform (composition of linear functions is linear). Non-linearity is what lets MLPs approximate arbitrary functions.

cards.front: Parameters in a Linear(in, out) layer?
cards.back: in × out + out (weight matrix + bias vector). E.g., Linear(1024, 4096) = 4,198,400 params.

cards.front: What does a Conv2d layer compute?
cards.back: Spatial cross-correlation between a learned kernel and input feature map. Translation-equivariant by design — same pattern detected anywhere in the image.

cards.front: Why do residual (skip) connections matter?
cards.back: They let gradients flow directly past layers (∂L/∂x = ∂L/∂y · (1 + ∂F/∂x)), preventing vanishing gradients in deep nets. Enabled training networks 100+ layers deep (ResNet).

cards.front: LayerNorm formula
cards.back: LN(x) = γ · (x − μ) / √(σ² + ε) + β with μ,σ computed across the feature dim per token. Stabilizes activations independent of batch size.

cards.front: BatchNorm vs LayerNorm — when to use which?
cards.back: BatchNorm: stats across the batch dim — fine for CNNs, bad for variable-length sequences and small batches. LayerNorm: stats per-sample across features — standard in Transformers.

cards.front: Embedding layer — what is it?
cards.back: Lookup table mapping discrete IDs → dense vectors. vocab_size × d_model trainable params. For Llama-2-7B: 32k × 4096 ≈ 130M params just in embeddings.

cards.front: LSTM solved what problem of vanilla RNN?
cards.back: Vanishing gradients over long sequences. The gated cell state allows information to flow unchanged across many steps when the forget gate is open.

cards.front: Why did Transformers replace RNN/LSTM for language?
cards.back: RNNs are inherently sequential (step t needs step t-1). Transformers compute all positions in parallel via attention, fully exploiting GPU/TPU matmul throughput.

cards.front: Sigmoid formula and range
cards.back: σ(x) = 1 / (1 + e⁻ˣ), range (0, 1). Used as gates in LSTMs and as binary-classification output.

cards.front: Tanh vs Sigmoid — why prefer tanh in hidden layers?
cards.back: Tanh is zero-centered (range −1..1) so gradients don't systematically push weights in one direction. Sigmoid (range 0..1) causes zigzag updates.

cards.front: ReLU formula and main advantage
cards.back: ReLU(x) = max(0, x). Gradient is exactly 0 or 1 → no vanishing in positive region, cheap to compute, sparse activations.

cards.front: "Dying ReLU" — what is it?
cards.back: A neuron whose inputs land in the negative region permanently outputs 0, and its gradient is 0 → never updates again. Fixes: Leaky ReLU, GELU, smaller LR, better init.

cards.front: GELU vs ReLU — why Transformers use GELU
cards.back: GELU(x) ≈ x · Φ(x) — smooth, non-monotonic, has small negative values that keep gradient flowing. Empirically ~0.5% perplexity improvement over ReLU at zero cost.

cards.front: SwiGLU formula and where it's used
cards.back: SwiGLU(x) = (xW · σ(xV)) · xU — three projections instead of two. Used in Llama, PaLM, Mistral FFN blocks. ~1% perplexity gain over GELU but +50% FFN params.

cards.front: What does backpropagation actually do?
cards.back: Applies the chain rule to compute ∂L/∂θ for every parameter θ in one backward pass through the computation graph. Time complexity equal to forward pass.

cards.front: MSE loss formula
cards.back: MSE = (1/N) Σ (ŷᵢ − yᵢ)². Standard for regression; penalizes large errors quadratically.

cards.front: Cross-entropy loss for classification
cards.back: CE = −Σ yᵢ log(p̂ᵢ). Reduces to −log p̂_correct for one-hot labels. Pairs with softmax; gradient is simply (p̂ − y).

cards.front: Binary cross-entropy formula
cards.back: BCE = −[y log p̂ + (1−y) log(1−p̂)]. Used with sigmoid output for binary classification or multi-label.

cards.front: KL divergence — what does it measure and is it symmetric?
cards.back: KL(P‖Q) = Σ P(x) log(P(x)/Q(x)) — extra bits needed to encode P using Q. Asymmetric: KL(P‖Q) ≠ KL(Q‖P).

cards.front: Focal loss — what problem does it solve?
cards.back: Focal = −(1−p̂)^γ log p̂. Down-weights easy examples (high p̂) so training focuses on hard ones. Used for class-imbalanced detection (RetinaNet).

cards.front: Why use the chain rule in vectorized form (Jacobian-vector products)?
cards.back: Full Jacobians for deep nets are too big to materialize (millions × millions). Reverse-mode autodiff computes vᵀJ directly, one row of the Jacobian at a time.

cards.front: Gradient checkpointing — what does it trade?
cards.back: Trades ~30% extra FLOPs for ~70% less activation memory. Re-computes activations during backward pass instead of storing them. Essential for training 70B+ models.

cards.front: Vanishing vs exploding gradients — fixes?
cards.back: Vanishing: ReLU/GELU, residual connections, LayerNorm, careful init (Xavier/He). Exploding: gradient clipping (typ. clip_grad_norm at 1.0).

cards.front: Mixed precision training: what dtypes are typically used?
cards.back: bf16 for forward/backward compute, fp32 for the optimizer state and gradient accumulation. Bf16 keeps fp32's exponent range; fp16 doesn't and needs loss scaling.

cards.front: Vanilla SGD update rule
cards.back: θ ← θ − η · ∇L(θ). Simple, no state. Noisy gradients can help escape saddle points.

cards.front: SGD with momentum — what does momentum buy you?
cards.back: v ← βv + ∇L; θ ← θ − ηv. Smooths the gradient trajectory, dampens oscillation in narrow ravines, accelerates along consistent directions.

cards.front: Adam update rule (high-level)
cards.back: Maintains running 1st moment m (mean of grads) and 2nd moment v (mean of grad²); update is θ ← θ − η · m̂ / (√v̂ + ε). Per-parameter adaptive LR.

cards.front: AdamW vs Adam — what changes?
cards.back: AdamW decouples weight decay from the gradient: applies decay directly to weights instead of adding L2 to the gradient. Standard for Transformers since 2019.

cards.front: Adam optimizer state memory cost per parameter (fp32)
cards.back: 8 bytes/param — 4 bytes for m, 4 bytes for v. Combined with fp32 weights (4) + grads (4) = 16 bytes/param. 70B model needs ~1 TB optimizer state alone.

cards.front: Lion optimizer — what makes it cheap?
cards.back: Uses only sign(gradient_momentum) for the update. 4 bytes/param state (half of Adam). Discovered via symbolic search (Chen et al. 2023). Often matches AdamW on LLMs.

cards.front: Adafactor — why use it instead of Adam at scale?
cards.back: Factorizes the 2nd moment matrix into row and column statistics → O(d) instead of O(d²) memory. Used in T5, PaLM. Standard on TPU.

cards.front: Typical LLM training schedule recipe
cards.back: AdamW (β₁=0.9, β₂=0.95, wd=0.1), linear warmup over 1-2% of steps, cosine decay to 10% of peak LR, gradient clipping at 1.0.

cards.front: Why does Adam need warmup at the start of training?
cards.back: Early on, bias-correction of v̂ is unreliable (tiny denominator) → effective LR spikes → divergence. Warmup gives v̂ time to stabilize.

cards.front: What β₁ and β₂ control in Adam
cards.back: β₁ (0.9): momentum decay for 1st moment (gradient mean). β₂ (0.999 default, 0.95 for LLMs): decay for 2nd moment (gradient variance estimate).

cards.front: Scaled dot-product attention formula
cards.back: Attn(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k) · V. Q,K,V are projections of the input; √d_k prevents softmax saturation at large d.

cards.front: Why divide by √d_k in attention?
cards.back: For random Q,K with unit variance, QKᵀ has variance d_k. Without scaling, softmax inputs grow with d_k and saturate (gradient → 0).

cards.front: Memory complexity of vanilla self-attention
cards.back: O(N² · d) activations for sequence length N — the QKᵀ matrix dominates. For N=8192, d=128, fp16: 256 MB just for one attention map.

cards.front: Multi-Head Attention (MHA) — why multiple heads?
cards.back: Each head learns different relationship types (syntax, coreference, position). With h heads of dim d_k = d_model/h, total params equal a single d_model×d_model projection.

cards.front: MQA vs GQA vs MHA — KV cache size?
cards.back: MHA: N heads of K,V → full cache. MQA: 1 shared K,V → N× smaller cache. GQA: groups of heads share K,V → tunable middle ground. Llama-2-70B uses GQA-8.

cards.front: FlashAttention — what does it do?
cards.back: Tiles attention into SRAM blocks and computes softmax online (running max + denom), avoiding materialization of the N×N attention matrix. O(N) memory, ~2× speed.

cards.front: Causal mask — why and how?
cards.back: For autoregressive LMs, position i can only attend to positions ≤ i. Implemented as adding −∞ to softmax logits above the diagonal before softmax.

cards.front: Sliding-window attention — what is it?
cards.back: Each token attends only to the last W tokens (Mistral uses W=4096). Reduces N² to N·W. Combined with global tokens (Longformer) or layer-wise W growth.

cards.front: RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding) — basic idea
cards.back: Rotates Q and K vectors by an angle proportional to position before attention. Relative position emerges from the dot product. Standard in Llama, Mistral, Qwen.

cards.front: FFN block in a Transformer — params and shape
cards.back: Two linear layers with non-linearity: d → 4d → d (vanilla) or d → 8d/3 → d (SwiGLU). 8d² params dominate Transformer parameter count.

cards.front: Attention vs FFN — which has more params in modern LLMs?
cards.back: FFN dominates (~2/3 of params). For Llama-2-70B: attention ≈ 19B params, FFN ≈ 47B params.

cards.front: Pre-norm vs post-norm in Transformer blocks
cards.back: Pre-norm (LN before sublayer): trains stably without warmup, used in GPT-2+, Llama. Post-norm (original Transformer): better final quality but unstable, needs warmup.

cards.front: Why have a KV cache at all?
cards.back: Decoder is autoregressive — token t needs attention over tokens 1..t. Without cache, each new token re-computes K,V for all previous tokens → O(N²) per step.

cards.front: KV cache size formula (bytes)
cards.back: 2 · B · H · S · d_head · bytes(dtype) — factor of 2 for K and V. For Llama-70B fp16 (B=1, H=64 GQA-8, S=4096, d=128): ~672 MB per request.

cards.front: Why is KV cache often the inference bottleneck?
cards.back: Per-token decode is memory-bound — must read full KV cache from HBM every step. Compute is small (one Q vector). Bandwidth, not FLOPs, sets throughput.

cards.front: PagedAttention — what problem does it solve?
cards.back: KV cache fragmentation. Allocates KV in fixed 16-token physical pages with per-request virtual page tables (OS-style). ~4× more concurrent requests than contiguous allocation.

cards.front: Continuous batching — what is it?
cards.back: Instead of static batches, the server adds new requests and evicts finished ones at every decode step. Massive throughput win for variable-length generation.

cards.front: Prefix caching — when does it help?
cards.back: Reuses KV for shared prefixes (system prompt, few-shot examples). Saves prefill compute for every request sharing the prefix. Standard in vLLM, sgLang, TGI.

cards.front: Speculative decoding — basic mechanism
cards.back: A small "draft" model proposes N tokens; the big model verifies all N in one forward pass and accepts the longest matching prefix. 2-3× faster decode if draft is accurate.

cards.front: KV cache quantization to int8 — what do you save and lose?
cards.back: 2× smaller cache at typically 0.1-0.3 ppl penalty. Big throughput win for memory-bound decode. Common: per-tensor symmetric quantization, dequant in the attention kernel.

cards.front: vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang — which problem do they solve?
cards.back: High-throughput LLM serving: continuous batching + PagedAttention + tensor parallelism + quantization. Open-source: vLLM, TGI, SGLang. NVIDIA: TensorRT-LLM.

cards.front: Prefill vs decode — what's the difference?
cards.back: Prefill: single forward pass over the full prompt, compute-bound, fills the KV cache. Decode: one token at a time, memory-bound, reads the cache.

cards.front: CUDA thread hierarchy
cards.back: Thread → Warp (32) → Block (≤1024) → Grid. A warp executes in lockstep on one SM. A block runs on one SM; multiple blocks form a grid.

cards.front: What is an SM (Streaming Multiprocessor)?
cards.back: A NVIDIA GPU's core compute unit. H100 has 132 SMs; each has CUDA cores + tensor cores + warp schedulers + shared memory.

cards.front: HBM vs SRAM bandwidth (H100)
cards.back: HBM3: ~3 TB/s. On-chip SRAM (shared memory + L1): ~33 TB/s per SM. ~10× ratio explains why kernel fusion matters so much.

cards.front: cuBLAS, cuDNN, NCCL — what does each do?
cards.back: cuBLAS: dense linear algebra (matmul). cuDNN: deep-learning primitives (conv, pool, attention). NCCL: collectives (all-reduce, all-gather) across GPUs/nodes.

cards.front: Triton — what is it and why use it?
cards.back: Python-embedded DSL for writing GPU kernels at block-level abstraction. Compiles to PTX. Used for FlashAttention, fused MoE, custom ops. Easier than raw CUDA C++.

cards.front: CUDA Graphs — what problem do they solve?
cards.back: Eliminates per-kernel launch overhead (~5-10 µs each) by recording a sequence of kernels and replaying as a single graph launch. Big win for small ops at low batch size.

cards.front: TensorRT-LLM — what is it?
cards.back: NVIDIA's LLM inference engine: fused kernels + in-flight batching + INT8/FP8 + speculative decoding. Often fastest single-GPU serving for NVIDIA hardware.

cards.front: Tensor cores — what do they do?
cards.back: Hardware units that execute 4×4 or 16×16 matmul-accumulate per cycle. H100 fp16: ~989 TFLOPS via tensor cores vs ~67 TFLOPS via CUDA cores. Use them or lose 15×.

cards.front: CUTLASS — what is it for?
cards.back: NVIDIA's C++ template library for composable matmul/conv kernels. Building block for cuBLAS/cuDNN and custom high-performance code. Source-level access to tensor cores.

cards.front: Memory-bound vs compute-bound kernels — how to tell?
cards.back: Compare achieved FLOP/byte to the device's ridge point (arithmetic intensity, roofline). H100: ridge ≈ 989/3 ≈ 330 FLOP/byte. Below → memory-bound; above → compute-bound.

cards.front: What is the MXU (Matrix eXtended Unit)?
cards.back: TPU's systolic array for matmul. v4: 128×128, v5p: 256×256. Streams data through PEs row-by-row, accumulating dot products with zero off-chip traffic during the matmul.

cards.front: bfloat16 — bit layout and why TPUs prefer it
cards.back: 1 sign + 8 exponent + 7 mantissa bits. Same exponent range as fp32 → no loss scaling needed. Lower mantissa precision is fine for training.

cards.front: JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch-XLA — what are they to TPUs?
cards.back: High-level frontends that lower to XLA HLO (intermediate representation) → TPU machine code. JAX is the de facto default for new TPU work.

cards.front: What is XLA?
cards.back: Accelerated Linear Algebra compiler. Takes HLO, performs whole-program operator fusion + layout assignment + auto-sharding (GSPMD), emits device code for TPU/GPU/CPU.

cards.front: Pallas — what is it?
cards.back: JAX's Triton-like DSL for writing custom TPU/GPU kernels in Python. Lowers to Mosaic (TPU) or Triton (GPU). Used when XLA fusion isn't aggressive enough.

cards.front: GSPMD — what does it do?
cards.back: Auto-sharding: propagates user-annotated sharding (on a few tensors) through the whole XLA graph. Enables data + tensor + pipeline parallel with minimal code.

cards.front: TPU pod vs slice vs chip
cards.back: Chip: 1 device (2 TensorCores in v4). Slice: a contiguous subset of a pod, the unit you allocate. Pod: a full physical install (v4 = 4096 chips with optical interconnect).

cards.front: ICI vs NVLink — what are they?
cards.back: Inter-chip interconnects. NVLink/NVSwitch (NVIDIA): 900 GB/s all-to-all in an 8-GPU node. ICI (TPU): toroidal mesh, ~100 GB/s per link, scales to pod-wide 3D torus.

cards.front: Nsight Systems vs Nsight Compute
cards.back: Nsight Systems (nsys): timeline view, CPU+GPU+NCCL+CUDA API — find the bottleneck. Nsight Compute (ncu): per-kernel deep dive — occupancy, memory throughput, instruction mix.

cards.front: torch.profiler — what does it give you?
cards.back: PyTorch-native timeline: op-level CPU/GPU time, memory snapshots, stack traces. Exports Chrome trace JSON. Best first-pass tool before reaching for nsys.

cards.front: What does MFU mean and what's a good target on H100?
cards.back: Model FLOPs Utilization = achieved / peak dense FLOPs. H100 bf16 peak ≈ 989 TF/s. Target ≥ 50% (~500 TF/s sustained) for healthy LLM training.

cards.front: Roofline model — what does it tell you?
cards.back: Plots achievable performance vs arithmetic intensity. Below the ridge point (FLOP/byte = peak_FLOPS / peak_BW) → memory-bound; above → compute-bound. Diagnoses ceilings.

cards.front: Why call torch.cuda.synchronize() before timing?
cards.back: CUDA kernel launches are asynchronous. Without sync, time.perf_counter measures launch-queue time, not work time. Always synchronize before t0 and before t1.

cards.front: XLA Profiler / TensorBoard profile tab — what's it for?
cards.back: JAX/TF's equivalent of torch.profiler. Captures HLO ops, TPU MXU utilization, host↔device transfers. Reads through TensorBoard with profile plugin.

cards.front: Bandwidth hierarchy (rough order, fastest first)
cards.back: HBM (~3 TB/s) > NVLink (~900 GB/s/node) > PCIe Gen5 (~64 GB/s) > InfiniBand NDR (~50 GB/s/port) > Ethernet (~12 GB/s for 100GbE).

cards.front: NVSwitch — what is it?
cards.back: NVIDIA's on-node crossbar that gives all-to-all 900 GB/s between 8 GPUs in a DGX. Without it, NVLink would be point-to-point ring.

cards.front: Ring all-reduce — bandwidth optimality
cards.back: Each GPU sends only 2(N-1)/N · size bytes regardless of N → bandwidth-optimal. NCCL's default for medium-size buffers across GPUs.

cards.front: Tree all-reduce vs Ring all-reduce
cards.back: Tree: O(log N) latency, used for small messages. Ring: O(N) latency but bandwidth-optimal, used for large messages. NCCL picks per buffer size.

cards.front: InfiniBand NDR — bandwidth per port
cards.back: 400 Gb/s = 50 GB/s per port. Rail-optimized fat-tree is the standard topology for AI training clusters.

cards.front: RDMA — what is it and why required for training?
cards.back: Remote Direct Memory Access: NIC reads/writes peer memory bypassing OS and CPU. Zero-copy, sub-µs latency — required for fast collectives. Used by IB and RoCE.

cards.front: GPUDirect RDMA — what does it add?
cards.back: NIC reads/writes GPU HBM directly over PCIe, bypassing system memory. Required to fully exploit IB bandwidth for inter-node all-reduce.

cards.front: Tensor Parallel vs Pipeline Parallel vs Data Parallel
cards.back: TP: split one matmul across GPUs (high comm, intra-node). PP: split layers across GPUs (low comm, micro-batches). DP: replicate model, split batch.

cards.front: FSDP / ZeRO-3 — what does it shard?
cards.back: Params + grads + optimizer state are each sharded across DP ranks. Each rank holds 1/N of everything. Materialized on-the-fly for compute via all-gather.

cards.front: OCS (Optical Circuit Switch) in TPU pods
cards.back: Reconfigurable optical interconnect — lets Google rewire the pod topology per job. Avoids fixed-topology bottlenecks and enables sub-pod slicing.

cards.front: Perplexity formula
cards.back: PPL = exp(−(1/N) Σ log p(xₜ | x<ₜ)) — lower is better. Comparable only on the same dataset and tokenizer.

cards.front: Three tiers of LLM evaluation
cards.back: (1) Intrinsic: PPL, loss curves (cheap, noisy). (2) Behavioral: MMLU, HumanEval, MT-Bench (capability). (3) Online: human A/B, Arena (ground truth).

cards.front: LM-as-judge — what are the main biases?
cards.back: Position bias (judges prefer first / last), length bias (prefer longer), self-bias (GPT-4 prefers GPT-4-style). Mitigate: swap order + average, control length.

cards.front: Goodhart's Law in ML eval
cards.back: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." Once a benchmark is optimized for, it stops predicting general capability. Rotate benchmarks.

cards.front: Train-test contamination — what is it and how to mitigate?
cards.back: Test items appear in pretraining corpus → model "memorizes" answers. Fixes: time-stamped benchmarks (LiveCodeBench), private held-out sets, contamination audits.

cards.front: Why isn't lower perplexity always better?
cards.back: PPL only measures next-token likelihood. Saturates well before user-visible quality differences. Use behavioral evals (MMLU, MT-Bench) for real comparison.

cards.front: Online A/B testing — what statistical risks should you guard against?
cards.back: Multiple-metric inflation (Bonferroni or FDR correction), peeking (use sequential / always-valid tests), and variance (CUPED can reduce 30-50%).

cards.front: Safety evaluation — what does HarmBench / JailbreakBench measure?
cards.back: Attack-success rate of adversarial prompts → harmful generations. Tradeoff with over-refusal measured by XSTest / OR-Bench (model refuses benign requests).

cards.front: MMLU — what does it test?
cards.back: 57 academic subjects, 4-choice MCQ, ~14k items (Hendrycks 2020). Tests broad knowledge. Saturating: frontier models score 88-93%. Successor: MMLU-Pro (10 choices).

cards.front: HumanEval — formula for pass@k
cards.back: pass@k = 1 − C(n−c, k) / C(n, k) where n = samples generated, c = correct ones. 164 hand-written Python problems (Chen 2021).

cards.front: GSM8K — what is it and roughly what scores do frontier models reach?
cards.back: Grade-school math word problems, 8.5k items, Cobbe 2021. Frontier ≈ 95%. Standard CoT + maj@N self-consistency.

cards.front: Chatbot Arena — how does it produce a ranking?
cards.back: Crowd-sourced blind A/B pairwise votes → Bradley-Terry → Elo rating. Closest proxy to user preference. ~1M+ votes; new model needs weeks to stabilize.

cards.front: MT-Bench — what is it?
cards.back: 80 multi-turn prompts × 8 categories, scored 1-10 by GPT-4 judge. Strong correlation with Arena Elo at fraction of the cost. (Zheng et al. 2023)

cards.front: IFEval — what does it solve that MT-Bench doesn't?
cards.back: Tests verifiable instructions ("answer in exactly 3 sentences") with deterministic checker. Removes judge bias. Used in LLaMA-3 and Gemini reports.

cards.front: Why prefer LiveCodeBench over HumanEval for new models?
cards.back: HumanEval (2021) is in CommonCrawl → contaminated. LiveCodeBench uses time-stamped contest problems, slice by submission date for leak-resistant eval.

cards.front: MLPerf — what does it benchmark?
cards.back: Hardware: standardized models (BERT, GPT-3, LLaMA-2, ResNet) with audited time-to-target-accuracy (training) and qps@latency (inference). Apples-to-apples across vendors.
